title: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
desc: Advocates sustained learning, implementation support and public-interest participation rather than waiting for technological certainty.

kps.k: The cluster advances an engagement-first position: lawyers should help shape AI’s use rather than wait for technological change to settle.
kps.d: Jen Leonard and Bridget McCormack frame AI literacy, experimentation and collaboration as ways to retain professional influence and pursue better client service. Their argument is not simply that adoption is inevitable, but that disengagement leaves others to determine its direction. Nik Reed similarly combines encouragement to experiment with caution. This is chiefly an agenda for professional action, supported by experience and institutional reasoning rather than demonstrated benefits. The supplied discussions acknowledge uncertainty and difficult transitions; they do not establish an ethical duty to use AI.

qs.q: So I’d rather have the lawyers leading what this looks like in legal.
qs.a: AI and the Future of Legal Jobs: What Law Firms Must Do to Stay Competitive — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: To your point, that’s also an abdication of their ability to shape the future they want to see.
qs.a: Did AI Just Practice Law? The OpenAI Lawsuit + Legalweek 2026 — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: AI adoption requires organisational change and implementation support, not merely software procurement or one enthusiastic champion.
kps.d: The Legal Week discussion warns that colleagues may disengage when they assume a capable leader has adoption covered. The GCO 2030 host’s recap likewise rejects a single, plug-and-play adoption path. Nick Fleisher adds practical substance: embedded former lawyers and legal operations leaders identify useful applications, explain input requirements and teach capabilities and limits through office hours. McCormack argues that existing employee use gives organisations a reason to establish guidance even before leaders accept promised benefits. These accounts describe practices and proposed mechanisms, not measured implementation success.

qs.q: It's like the firm thinks it's all handled because Nora is on it (or some other fabulous – probably woman – is on it), and then they check out.
qs.a: Live from Legal Week 2025: Unveiling a New AI Course for Lawyers — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: It will require true planning, leadership, [music] and change management to succeed.
qs.a: Norie Campbell & Jen Ruddick — Thomson Reuters legal department (GCO 2030) · In-house counsel · 2026

kps.k: Practical learning should combine sustained use, relevant demonstrations and accessible professional education.
kps.d: Gabe Pereyra argues that repeated hands-on use builds a mental model that guides alone cannot provide. McCormack recommends demonstrations on work hesitant users care about, while the hosts promote courses, peer exchange and expert commentary for time-constrained practitioners. Legal-education discussions challenge blanket AI prohibitions as potentially inconsistent with evolving client expectations, while retaining accreditation constraints. Leonard also proposes tailored learning for solos and small firms and programming through women’s legal networks. Her observations about access and gender remain tentative: the excerpts establish neither a measured adoption gap nor its causes.

qs.q: You can give people guides and best practices, but it’s like teaching someone to use an iPhone—you only really learn by using it every day.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: But if they see something applied to work they personally care about, it can change everything.
qs.a: Future-Proofing Your Law Firm: Lessons from AI Benchmarking — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The proposed professional response shifts value toward strategic advice, client relationships and newly possible work.
kps.d: Leonard distinguishes generative AI from earlier digitisation because it can perform work that lawyers currently regard as their contribution. McCormack envisages AI organising legal sources while lawyers advise clients creatively and strategically. Wider public access to information could also make lawyers interpreters of outside advice, including explanations of its errors, rather than exclusive information providers. Zach Abramowitz extends the ambition beyond faster existing workflows to capabilities firms have not yet imagined. Better service, broader capacity and more enjoyable practice remain prospective benefits, not established productivity, employment or well-being outcomes.

qs.q: But to your point, it's not helpful in understanding the nature of what this technology is and what it means for lawyers—because it's not just digitizing or automating things we used to do in an analog world.
qs.a: AI in Legal Research: The Battle Over Copyright and Innovation — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: There will be some who welcome the extra help (even if sometimes the extra help isn’t quite right), and who welcome the opportunity to explain why.
qs.a: AI Revolution in 2025? What Lawyers Missed Over the Holidays — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The public-interest case concerns meaningful participation and greater service capacity, not guaranteed victories or elimination of unmet need.
kps.d: McCormack advocates trial-court tools because crowded dockets and unaffordable representation exceed lawyers’ capacity to respond. David Slayton defines the goal as reducing barriers and enabling informed participation, explicitly allowing that users may still lose. The AI for Justice closing discussion similarly treats reducing unmet need as worthwhile without promising to close the justice gap. Government access to tools and reconsideration of court processes appear as practical conditions. A reported tenant appeal win motivates experimentation, but does not establish that trial-stage AI would have changed the outcome; the supplied legal-aid excerpt provides no quantitative impact finding.

qs.q: So the “think bigger” part of me was like, this is really exciting – let’s give this technology to the trial courts, where judges are trying to juggle so many cases with so many litigants (many of whom will never be able to afford lawyers).
qs.a: Can AI Help You Win in Court? A New Era of Self-Representation — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: You may lose even with all that information, we're not saying we want to make people win or lose; we want to give them information.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The main tensions concern risk, professional purpose and the conditions for responsible experimentation, rather than a developed contest between opposing camps.
kps.d: The hosts report resistance prompted by hallucinations and public-interest lawyers’ concerns about high-stakes housing and family matters. Leonard answers the latter with augmentation that preserves lawyers’ time with clients, not wholesale replacement. Other excerpts acknowledge harmful uses, security and compliance, and the difference between judicial goodwill and product endorsement. Yet invitations to experiment sometimes precede specified safeguards. The material therefore records concerns and proposed responses without resolving reliability questions or establishing that optimistic framing overcomes practical risks.

qs.q: They’ll shut down pretty quickly when they hear about hallucinations and think, “Well, this isn’t ready for prime time.
qs.a: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: I would say a lot of the skepticism I get in presentations comes from public-interest lawyers – understandably – and their pushback is sort of that they're dealing with the most precious parts of people's lives (whether that's housing or their family members).
qs.a: Live from Legal Week 2025: Unveiling a New AI Course for Lawyers — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Professional participation extends to governance: rules, standards and institutional design should develop deliberately and with broader input.
kps.d: McCormack criticises litigation-led regulation because resources shape which disputes reach courts and courts address only the questions presented. She favours deliberate public policymaking and predicts state variation in defining unauthorized practice; the OpenAI lawsuit remains an allegation with an unknown outcome in the excerpt. Leonard separately treats the bar opinions discussed as nonbinding planning resources. Proposals include convening educators, firms, regulators, judges and the public, and inviting general counsel involved in agentic commerce to contribute to the LCP. These are governance recommendations, not settled rules or completed reforms.

qs.q: So if that becomes your regulatory mechanism, you’re getting a skewed sample of disputes.
qs.a: Did AI Just Practice Law? The OpenAI Lawsuit + Legalweek 2026 — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: And not binding, like we said, but really a thoughtful way to begin strategizing around your own practice's response—your own firm's response.
qs.a: Generative AI in Legal Practice: Adapting to New Ethical Standards and Regulations — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The evidentiary contribution is mainly an agenda for learning and testing; enthusiasm, demonstrations and announcements do not establish effectiveness.
kps.d: Much of the supplied material consists of introductions and closing exchanges, often from the same hosts. Research references omit findings, demonstrations report reactions without accuracy checks, and product discussions announce plans rather than validated results. For example, the DeepResearch eviction-law demonstration does not establish equivalence to academic research, while AAA’s promised independent white paper does not itself establish arbitrator reliability. The speakers also call for stronger evidence: measuring lawyers’ effectiveness, revisiting forecasts and reassessing research baselines as technology changes. Repeated optimism should therefore remain attributed opinion, not cumulative proof.

qs.q: So up until now, our conversations have been amazing, but they have just been the two of us really riffing on our thoughts and opinions about the changing landscape of AI in the law.
qs.a: A New Name, A New Era: Welcome to AI and the Future of Law — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: She was stunned—literally calling over her partner, amazed at what she was seeing.

vlens.an: The usable legal-tech-vendor evidence generally shifts the emphasis from lawyers collectively shaping AI’s professional and public-interest direction to practical adoption and provider-side delivery. Nik Reed aligns with the proposition’s engagement-first core by recommending experimentation tempered by caution, but offers no concrete account of lawyer-led governance, implementation support or public-interest participation. The Clio leaders instead foreground rapid product execution, security, compliance and anticipated product maturity—a constructive but materially different vendor-execution framing. The other two excerpts are closing remarks that establish only interest in, or recognition of, technological change and cannot substantiate the featured individuals’ positions. Thus, among this curated selection, the clearest common thread is active movement under uncertainty, while material variation lies between cautious user experimentation and vendor-led product execution; neither provides broad support for the proposition’s fuller agenda of lawyer-led institutional governance.

qs.q: I will also say secure and compliant because John doesn't want to think about that.
qs.a: Inside Clio's AI-Driven Transformation: CPO John Foreman and CTO Jonathan Watson · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: The academia-and-research voice accepts the proposition’s engagement-first orientation and materially strengthens its evidentiary discipline. It argues that professional participation in AI deployment should be informed by research but should not freeze baseline findings into claims about current conditions, especially as the technology and its use evolve. This supports sustained learning and testing while reinforcing the cluster’s warning that enthusiasm and early evidence do not establish effectiveness. Internal variation is limited but material: the closing response emphasises continual reassessment and the temporal limits of baseline answers, whereas Jen Leonard stresses the practical value of otherwise scarce academic research for conversations with practitioners and leaders. Neither contribution supplies specific study results or demonstrates that AI deployment improves legal work.

qs.q: We need to be constantly reevaluating this and constantly asking these questions.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Our answers give us baselines, but they don’t tell us where we are.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The substantive contribution from this curated professional voice accepts the engagement-first proposition and extends it with concrete institutional priorities: legal education should prepare future lawyers for AI-enabled client expectations, and governance should involve regulators, the judiciary and the public alongside law schools and law firms. The reasoning is prospective and institutional rather than evidence of successful implementation. Material internal variation limits the breadth of this conclusion: one excerpt contains only closing remarks, while Nikki Shaver’s forecast about Harvey and Claude concerns likely market architecture and is adjacent to, but does not itself endorse, active professional participation. Thus, the voice builds on the proposition where it addresses it substantively, without implying that all included sources take that position.

qs.q: And I think if you look at how law schools are approaching the use of AI — how many are prohibiting the use of AI — I think if you spell that out and think about how client-centric you can be as a counselor to your STEM clients, eventually it’s just a nonsensical approach to being able to keep up with what your clients will expect from you.
qs.a: Inside Legal Innovation: AI Adoption with Jae Um & Ilona Logvinova — full episode transcript · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: We talked about two stakeholders primarily — law schools and law firms — but what about the regulators, the judiciary, the public (who never gets a voice in how law is effectuated)?
qs.a: Inside Legal Innovation: AI Adoption with Jae Um & Ilona Logvinova — full episode transcript · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The curated sources in the regulators, courts and professional-bodies voice accept the cluster’s engagement-first proposition and materially develop its institutional dimension. Their common reasoning is that lawyers and legal institutions retain influence only by becoming sufficiently informed to participate in deployment and rule-setting; that adoption requires organisational strategy, training and implementation expertise rather than software procurement alone; and that courts and public bodies should connect technology adoption with process redesign and access-to-justice goals. Concrete extensions include using nonbinding bar guidance as a planning resource, embedding legal and legal-operations specialists in implementation, involving users in system development, disclosing safeguards, engaging general counsel in standards work, and reconsidering court processes alongside new tools. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary strength. Some sources offer specific governance or deployment mechanisms, while many provide broad encouragement, predictions, personal demonstrations or planned initiatives rather than measured outcomes. Public-interest and judicial sources generally favour augmentation and informed participation, not guaranteed victories or wholesale replacement, and acknowledge high-stakes risks; however, safeguards are sometimes promised rather than specified or validated. A few introductory excerpts are too limited to establish a position at all, particularly those merely announcing discussions of judicial drafting, ethics, forecasts or cross-disciplinary studies. This internal variation does not amount to opposition: where a substantive position is supplied, it predominantly advances deliberate professional participation while preserving uncertainty about effectiveness and responsible deployment conditions.

qs.q: Lawyers are needed to help figure out what the regulation should be.
qs.a: Did AI Just Practice Law? The OpenAI Lawsuit + Legalweek 2026 — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: So as we think about embracing these things and re-looking at our processes to make things work better, to me that's the most exciting thing that keeps me going every day.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The AI-native legal provider source supports the proposition’s engagement-first orientation, but does not materially extend it. Jen Leonard links the provider’s work to openness about what legal innovation can make possible and to the profession’s underlying purpose, aligning with the view that lawyers should participate in shaping AI rather than wait for certainty. The source also presents cautious judicial goodwill as compatible with responsible experimentation. Material variation lies in the strength and status of these claims: Leonard’s praise is explicitly enthusiastic but qualified as a possibly oversimplified interpretation, while the account of judicial sentiment is second-hand and carefully distinguishes receptiveness from endorsement of a private product. The evidence therefore indicates supportive professional and institutional attitudes, not demonstrated effectiveness, formal judicial approval or a detailed implementation model. Because this is a single curated source, it should not be treated as representative of AI-native legal providers generally.

qs.q: I certainly don't have the expertise that either of you have—and this may be an oversimplification—but I think Bridget would share the takeaway that throughout our conversations with great people doing innovative things, the through-line is mindset around what's possible and the reason we're all part of this profession and what we're trying to do.

vlens.an: This access-to-justice and civil-society source supports the proposition’s engagement-first stance, particularly its public-interest dimension. It argues for continuing to develop and expand legal-AI applications because even a partial reduction in unmet legal need would be worthwhile; technological uncertainty and the possibility that the justice gap will remain are treated as reasons for realistic expectations, not for disengagement. The source’s forward-looking expectation that evolving technology will enable additional use cases also aligns with sustained experimentation rather than waiting for the technology to settle. Its support is narrower than the full proposition, however: it does not address lawyer-led governance, organisational implementation, verification or safeguards. There is some internal variation between pragmatic near-term ambition—changing the justice gap’s trajectory—and optimism about future capabilities, but neither strand opposes professional engagement. The excerpt supplies no quantitative evidence that technology has reduced unmet need, so these claims remain an agenda and prediction rather than a demonstrated impact finding. As this is a curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of all access-to-justice or civil-society professionals.

qs.q: So as Laura mentioned, we may not be able to close our gap, but you can certainly take a  bigger bite with technology.

qs.q: And then we just amplify further and further these use cases and the ones that  will be available to us in a year and two years and three years that aren't possible today because the technology itself continues to evolve.

vlens.an: The in-house counsel and legal-operations source supports the cluster’s principal engagement-first proposition by presenting AI deployment as an organisational change process that legal-department leaders must actively shape, rather than as passive procurement of a plug-and-play tool. Its reasons are practical: adoption paths differ across departments, people must be brought through the transition, and success requires planning, leadership and change management. Internal variation is limited but material: the source combines rejection of a single adoption path with a positive account of the organisational capabilities needed for implementation. Its contribution is narrower than the full cluster proposition because it does not address public-interest participation, professional governance or sustained hands-on learning, and it offers closing observations rather than empirical evidence of successful adoption. As this is a curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of in-house counsel or legal-operations professionals generally.

vlens.an: The selected traditional-law-firm sources support the proposition that lawyers should engage actively in shaping AI deployment rather than wait for certainty. Their common rationale is practical: experimentation, peer exchange and accessible expert commentary can build professional understanding, while collaboration with startups can help firms identify uses beyond merely accelerating existing workflows. Both also associate engagement with prospective improvements in client service and legal practice. There is material variation in emphasis: the Quinn Emanuel discussion focuses on an experimentation-friendly culture and informal continuing education, whereas Abramowitz stresses external startup partnerships and the development of previously unimagined capabilities. The sources remain cautious at the evidentiary level: claimed benefits are experiential or predictive, and Abramowitz explicitly describes the more ambitious “2.0” opportunity as only nascent. Thus, they support an engagement-first agenda without demonstrating that experimentation or partnership has yet produced reliable organisational outcomes. Because these are curated sources, this position should not be generalized to traditional law firms as a whole.

qs.q: It’s been such a fun conversation, and I’m really, really grateful to both of you for coming on — and grateful to Quinn for fostering such a great culture that allows this kind of experimentation.

qs.a: How BigLaw Can and Should Partner with Early-Stage Startups · Law firms · 2025

elens.an: Across this curated 2023–2024 set, the sources support the proposition that lawyers should engage early and help shape AI deployment rather than wait for technological certainty. Their recurring reasons are that legal professionals need accessible, sustained AI literacy; hands-on experimentation can reveal useful applications; employee use makes organisational strategy and guidance urgent; and professional institutions—including bars, law schools, courts and practitioner networks—can influence implementation in the public interest. Material variation concerns the form and strength of engagement. Some sources concentrate on education for solos, small firms or women’s legal networks; others advocate firm-level strategy, bar-guided governance, civil-justice collaboration or AI-enabled legal education. The law-school discussion makes the clearest concrete extension by assigning deans and cross-institutional partnerships an implementation role. Two excerpts remain unclear because they merely introduce judicial drafting or medical comparisons without reaching a substantive position. Optimistic claims about better well-being, broader capability, access to justice and institutional transformation are generally aspirations, predictions or anecdotes rather than demonstrated outcomes. Risk, hallucinations and difficult institutional change are acknowledged, but these caveats qualify responsible experimentation rather than amounting to opposition.

qs.q: Now it’s about the humans collaborating and coming up with innovative ways to make them work for good.
qs.a: How Will AI Tools Like ChatGPT 4.0 and Notebook LM Shape the Future of Law? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: And if you want to make sure they’re using it in ways you think are appropriate, it might make sense to figure out a strategy for your organization—and also think about the cost of not putting a strategy together.”  And I think people are convinced by that in a way they may not yet be convinced by some of the upside.
qs.a: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: Across this curated selection of 2025 sources, the predominant relationship to the proposition is supportive: lawyers and legal institutions are urged to engage with AI through experimentation, education, organisational change, implementation and public-interest participation rather than wait for the technology to stabilise. Common reasons include preserving professional influence over deployment, responding to changing client expectations, shifting lawyers’ value toward strategic and relational work, and expanding meaningful access to legal processes. Material variation concerns the form and conditions of engagement. Some sources focus narrowly on learning and experimentation; others develop organisational, educational, court-system or multi-stakeholder governance responses. Public-interest accounts qualify success as better participation or reduced unmet need, not guaranteed outcomes. Risk is generally treated as a reason for caution, safeguards, security, compliance and augmentation—not disengagement. One provider-side source redirects attention toward product execution, while excerpts containing only introductions or broad forecasts remain unclear. Most claims are recommendations, institutional plans, anecdotes or predictions rather than measured evidence that adoption is effective, safe or scalable, so the period supports an engagement-first agenda more strongly than it demonstrates its results. Because the corpus is curated, this pattern should not be treated as representative of all 2025 legal-sector opinion.

elens.an: The 2026 sources collectively accept the cluster’s engagement-first proposition and materially develop how lawyers should act on it. Their common rationale is that effective legal-AI deployment depends on professional participation rather than software procurement alone: sustained hands-on use builds proficiency; embedded legal and legal-operations expertise, training, leadership and change management support implementation; continual reassessment keeps practice responsive to changing evidence; and lawyers and general counsel should help design regulation and standards. Material variation lies in emphasis and evidentiary strength. Some sources focus on organisational implementation, others on individual reskilling, iterative competency frameworks or governance of unauthorized practice and agentic commerce. Prospective benefits such as higher-value work remain predictions, and most claims rest on experience, analogy or institutional reasoning rather than measured outcomes. Several excerpts are merely closing remarks or market forecasts and are too insubstantial or adjacent to establish a position. Because the corpus is curated, these relationships do not indicate how prevalent the view is among lawyers or other groups.
